\chapter{Five Words for How Something Feels}
\label{ch:seco-y-mojado}
\hlchaptermodality{379}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say seco, mojado, fresco, tibio and grueso, and count five things and say how each one feels.}

Complete ES-C379-grueso: count five things and say how each one feels, and say one thing about each.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[seco]{seco — the word on a wine label}

\label{lesson:ES-C379-seco}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the summit}, then \emph{the building}. (\emph{La cumbre}; \emph{El edificio}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el polvo — what a dry place makes.
  \item la arena — dry by definition.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{SE-co}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{c} before \emph{o} is a hard \emph{k}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{seco} — \textquotedblleft{}dry.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{siccus} was dry. English has it in \textbf{desiccate}, and French put it on a bottle: \emph{sec} on a wine label means the wine is not sweet.

Two further claims travel with this word, and they are worth separating, because one is true in a complicated way and the other may not be true at all.

\textbf{German \emph{Sekt}} really does descend from French \emph{sec}, borrowed in the seventeenth century. But in German it never meant dry. It named a \textbf{sweet} wine from southern Spain and the Canaries, and it became the word for sparkling wine by accident: German translators rendered Shakespeare's \emph{sack} as \emph{Sect}, and the story goes that in an 1825 Berlin tavern the actor Ludwig Devrient, still in character as Falstaff, demanded \textquotedblleft{}Sekt\textquotedblright{} and was served champagne.

Treat that last part as an anecdote. It is repeated everywhere and rests on very little. The borrowing itself is not in doubt; the tavern is.

\textbf{English \emph{sack}}, the old name for sherry, is usually filed under \emph{sec} too — and there the evidence gets thin. The Oxford dictionary admits it cannot explain the vowel, and the wine in question was sweet, which is awkward for a word meaning dry. Others propose Spanish \emph{sacar}, \textquotedblleft{}to draw out,\textquotedblright{} from the export trade. Unsettled.

So: \emph{seco}, \emph{desiccate} and \emph{sec} are secure. \emph{Sekt} is a genuine relative that changed jobs. \emph{Sack} is a maybe.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now describe a thing with no water in it: \emph{muy seco}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{seco}
  \item \emph{muy seco}
  \item \emph{un vino seco}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which English word means to dry something out completely? (\emph{Desiccate}.) And does German \emph{Sekt} mean dry? (No — sparkling, and the tavern story behind that shift is only a story.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mojado]{mojado — wet means softened}

\label{lesson:ES-C379-mojado}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the building}, then \emph{dry}. (\emph{El edificio}; \emph{Seco}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el agua — what does it.
  \item la toalla — what undoes it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mo-JA-do}, three beats with the weight on the middle one. The \emph{j} is a rasp from the back of the throat, and the \emph{d} between vowels is soft. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{mojado} — \textquotedblleft{}wet.\textquotedblright{}

\emph{Mojado} comes from \textbf{mojar}, and \emph{mojar} is Vulgar Latin \textbf{molliāre} — to soften, to make soft. Behind that is \textbf{mollis}, \textquotedblleft{}soft.\textquotedblright{}

So Spanish did not name wetness after water. It named it after what water \textbf{does}: bread goes soft, leather goes soft, earth goes soft. The word is about the result, not the substance.

English holds the same \emph{mollis} in two places, both of them still about softening:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item to \textbf{mollify} someone is to soften them;
  \item an \textbf{emollient} is a cream that softens skin.
\end{itemize}

Spanish keeps two more cousins nearby. A \textbf{muelle} is a spring — the soft, yielding thing in a mattress. And a \textbf{molusco} is a mollusc, an animal classified by its soft body.

The Academy's dictionary gives this chain without a single hedge, which is rarer than you might expect and worth noticing when it happens.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now describe something covered in water: \emph{muy mojado}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mojado}
  \item \emph{muy mojado}
  \item \emph{el papel está mojado}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{molliāre} mean? (To soften.) And which English cream is named from the same \emph{mollis}? (An emollient.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[fresco]{fresco — the word on a church ceiling}

\label{lesson:ES-C379-fresco}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{dry}, then \emph{wet}. (\emph{Seco}; \emph{Mojado}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el frío — the stronger version.
  \item el calor — what it relieves.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{FRES-co}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{fr} runs together, the \emph{r} is a single tap, and the \emph{c} before \emph{o} is a hard \emph{k}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{fresco} — \textquotedblleft{}cool.\textquotedblright{}

This one is Germanic. Some form of \textbf{frisk} — \textquotedblleft{}new, lively\textquotedblright{} — spread through Romance and settled in Spanish as \emph{fresco}. The Academy's dictionary does not say which Germanic language handed it over, and neither will anybody else with confidence.

English \textbf{fresh} has that same Germanic root, but it did not borrow it from Spanish or from French. It inherited it: Old English \textbf{fersc} meant \textquotedblleft{}unsalted.\textquotedblright{}

The interesting part is that Romance then came back and reshaped the English word anyway. The letters swapped places (\emph{fersc} to \emph{fresh}), and the senses spread out to \textquotedblleft{}new, pure, eager\textquotedblright{} — both changes probably under the influence of Old French \emph{fres}, which was the same Germanic word arriving from the other direction. So English kept its own root and borrowed its own word's shape.

And a \textbf{fresco} on a church ceiling is this word in Italian dress. The painter works \emph{a fresco}, on the fresh plaster, while it is still damp — the pigment sinks in and dries as part of the wall. Painting on plaster that has already set is a different technique with a different name.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now describe cool air: \emph{muy fresco}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{fresco}
  \item \emph{muy fresco}
  \item \emph{hace fresco}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \emph{fresco} Latin or Germanic? (Germanic.) And why is a fresco called that? (The paint goes onto fresh, still-wet plaster.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tibio]{tibio — one Latin word, two states of wear}

\label{lesson:ES-C379-tibio}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{wet}, then \emph{cool}. (\emph{Mojado}; \emph{Fresco}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el calor — the far end of it.
  \item la leche — the thing most often described this way.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{TI-bio}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{b} between vowels is soft, and the \emph{io} is one glide. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{tibio} — \textquotedblleft{}lukewarm.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{tepidus} meant lukewarm. Spanish has \emph{tibio}. English has \textbf{tepid}. They are the same word.

What separates them is not ancestry but \textbf{mileage}.

\emph{Tibio} travelled the long way: mouth to mouth, generation after generation, for two thousand years, and it wore down the way a stone step wears down. \emph{Tepid} took a shortcut. English lifted it out of written Latin around 1400, which is why it still looks like the original.

This is one of the most useful things to know about Romance vocabulary. When a Spanish word and an English word come from the same Latin but look different, the usual reason is that one was \textbf{spoken} the whole way and the other was \textbf{read} into existence much later.

A footnote for anyone checking the sound changes: the \emph{i} in \emph{tibio} is not what the ordinary rules predict — a short \emph{e} should have given \emph{ie}. Corominas explains it as the vowel being pulled upward by the glide that follows. Worth knowing so you do not use this word as your model.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now describe something neither hot nor cold: \emph{muy tibio}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tibio}
  \item \emph{muy tibio}
  \item \emph{la leche está tibia}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which English word is \emph{tibio}'s exact Latin twin? (\emph{Tepid}.) And why do they look so different? (One was spoken for two thousand years; the other was read out of a book around 1400.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[grueso]{grueso — the word behind grocer}

\label{lesson:ES-C379-grueso}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{cool}, then \emph{lukewarm}. (\emph{Fresco}; \emph{Tibio}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la manta — the thing you want to be thick.
  \item el hilo — the thing you want thin.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{GRUE-so}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{ue} is one glide, and the \emph{r} after the \emph{g} is a single tap. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{grueso} — \textquotedblleft{}thick.\textquotedblright{}

\textbf{Grossus} meant thick or coarse — and it is \textbf{Late} Latin, not classical. Cicero would not have used it, and where it came from before that is not known.

English took it through Old French as \textbf{gross}, which still carries both the old sense (a gross weight, the whole of it) and a newer disgusted one.

The better cousin is \textbf{grocer}. A grocer is not named for groceries. Medieval Latin \textbf{grossarius} meant a dealer who sold in \textbf{quantity} — wholesale, rather than a piece at a time. That is what the word says about the job: not what you sell, but the size you sell it in.

One tidy-looking bridge to refuse. English also has a noun \textbf{a gross}, meaning twelve dozen, and it is tempting to say a grocer is someone who sells \textquotedblleft{}by the gross.\textquotedblright{} That is a later and separate development, from a French phrase for a large dozen. The occupation came from the adjective, not from the counting word.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now describe something with weight to it: \emph{muy grueso}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{grueso}
  \item \emph{muy grueso}
  \item \emph{un libro grueso}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Was \emph{grossus} classical Latin? (No — Late Latin, and its own origin is unknown.) And what did a \emph{grossarius} sell? (Goods in bulk, rather than by the piece.)
\end{tcolorbox}
